prompt.context: The client is a pharmaceutical company with manufacturing plants in the US, Mexico and other locations. The client recently undertook a benchmarking exercise. They observed that one particular plant had very high per unit costs. This plant produced only one type of drug in three different types of packaging. This drug requires a unique manufacturing process. It is an OTC drug.
prompt.question: The management is trying to figure out what is driving such high unit costs and then what could be done about it.

clarifying_info.q: Where is the anomalous plant located?
clarifying_info.a: The plant is located in New Jersey.

clarifying_info.q: How do wage rates at this plant compare to other plants?
clarifying_info.a: Wage rates in New Jersey are about 40% higher.

clarifying_info.q: What is the utilization rate of this plant?
clarifying_info.a: Utilization in the New Jersey plant is about 33% of capacity.

clarifying_info.q: How do total costs compare to other plants?
clarifying_info.a: Total cost is at least double that of the other plants.
Variable costs are estimated to be at least 40-50% higher.

clarifying_info.q: How does direct labor cost compare?
clarifying_info.a: Cost of direct labor was 40% higher than other plants.
Worker productivity was comparable across plants.

clarifying_info.q: How do other variable costs compare (materials, admin, transport)?
clarifying_info.a: Other costs such as direct material, administrative, and transportation costs are comparable.

clarifying_info.q: What is the capacity utilization at other plants?
clarifying_info.a: Average utilization at other plants is about 70%. The New Jersey plant runs at 33%.
Cost allocation uses total fixed costs proportioned to the produced lot.

framework: 1. Analyze the cost structure of the anomalous plant vs. other plants (variable costs and fixed costs)
2. Investigate process-specific factors (labor rates, productivity, equipment setup, unique manufacturing process)
3. Examine capacity utilization (current vs. benchmark utilization and its impact on per-unit fixed cost allocation)

questions.prompt: What is driving the higher variable costs at the New Jersey plant?
questions.guidance: Labor is the key driver: NJ wage rates are ~40% higher than other locations, directly explaining the elevated direct labor cost (also ~40% higher). Worker productivity is comparable, so the issue is purely the wage rate differential, not efficiency. Other variable cost components (materials, admin, transport) are in line with other plants.

questions.prompt: What is driving the higher fixed costs per unit?
questions.guidance: The NJ plant operates at only 33% utilization versus the 70% average at other plants. Fixed costs are allocated per produced unit; at lower utilization, fixed costs are spread over fewer units, dramatically increasing the fixed cost per unit. This utilization gap is a major driver of total unit cost being at least double other plants.

math.setup: If total fixed costs = F, and average plant produces Q units at 70% utilization, NJ plant produces Q * (33/70) units. Per-unit fixed cost at NJ = F / (Q * 33/70) = F * 70 / (Q * 33), versus F / Q at average plant.
steps: Ratio of NJ per-unit fixed cost to average plant: (F / (Q*0.33)) / (F / (Q*0.70)) = 0.70 / 0.33 ≈ 2.12
So fixed costs per unit at NJ are approximately 2.1x those at the average plant
math.answer: NJ per-unit fixed costs are roughly 2.1x the average, due solely to low utilization.

questions.prompt: What solutions could reduce the high unit costs at the NJ plant?
questions.guidance: Candidates should brainstorm multiple levers before evaluating feasibility. Three main options: (1) Manufacture other drugs on the same line — not feasible because equipment is set up uniquely for this drug and cannot produce other company products; (2) Sell the plant and outsource production to a competitor — management rejected this because they did not want to lose control of manufacturing; (3) Enter a joint venture: sell the plant but contractually reserve ~40% of capacity for the company's own production. This raises utilization, lowers per-unit costs, and retains some manufacturing control. This is what the company actually implemented.

brainstorming.prompt: What are possible ways to reduce per-unit costs at the New Jersey plant?

categories.name: Increase utilization
ideas: Manufacture other products on the same line (ruled out — unique equipment)
Enter a joint venture to share capacity with another party
Find a contract manufacturing partner to fill idle capacity

categories.name: Reduce fixed costs
ideas: Sell the plant and lease back only the capacity needed
Consolidate production to another lower-cost plant (if feasible given unique process)

categories.name: Reduce variable costs
ideas: Negotiate lower wage rates or renegotiate labor contracts
Automate portions of the manufacturing process to reduce direct labor hours
Relocate production to a lower-wage location

categories.name: Outsourcing / divestiture
ideas: Sell plant and outsource production to a competitor (rejected — loss of control)
Joint venture: sell plant but retain 40% captive capacity in the contract (implemented solution)

recommendation: The primary cost drivers are (1) NJ labor rates ~40% above benchmark and (2) plant utilization of only 33% vs. 70% average, together causing total unit costs to be at least 2x those of comparable plants.

The recommended action is to enter a joint venture — sell the plant to a partner but contractually secure ~40% of capacity for the company's own production. This raises effective utilization, reduces per-unit fixed cost allocation, and preserves manufacturing control.
risks: Joint venture partner may not maintain quality or reliability standards for an OTC drug
Contractual capacity commitment may become insufficient if demand grows beyond 40%
Loss of full operational control could create supply disruption risk
next_steps: Identify and qualify potential joint venture partners
Negotiate capacity and quality terms in the JV contract
Model revised per-unit cost at higher utilization to confirm cost reduction target is met
Evaluate whether any variable cost reduction (e.g., automation) is complementary to the JV
